The event is rain or shine, with no registration required.
strings.这是过去的活动安排，不是当下的邀请，也不能证明活动后来实际怎样举行。照着公告改写: This is a past event schedule, not a current invitation, nor does it prove how the event actually took place later. Rewriting the invitation based on the announcement is only a learning exercise and does not imply NASA endorsement. When no target time zone is specified, do not convert EDT directly.
strings.伦敦国家美术馆：计划参观: The National Gallery, London: Plan Your Visit
strings.2026年9月18日查阅的官网资料。练习场景是假设，不是实时出行承诺。: Official website information accessed on 2026-9-18. The practice scenario is hypothetical, not a real-time travel commitment.
strings.作者描述了向一款广泛使用的聊天机器人询问某位研究人员的博士论文题目，却得到了数个: The author describes asking a widely used chatbot for the title of a researcher's doctoral dissertation, only to receive several confident yet distinct incorrect answers. The author distinguishes between correct answers and baseless guesses, and discusses evaluation incentives.
strings.切勿虚构错误的论文题目，也不要在文中未指名的情况下指认具体的聊天机器人。该示例仅: Do not fabricate incorrect dissertation titles, nor identify a specific chatbot if it is not named in the text. This example only confirms the reported failure case and does not represent a general error rate.

intro.situation: 小区发来停车施工通知。周日一早你要开车送妈妈去医院。车停在 A 区地面车位，平时走西门。你还写了段话，问要不要提前挪车、能不能走东门，也想知道下雨时该怎么办。
intro.need: 通知写了日期、区域、挪车时间和下雨安排。你想让 AI 先找出和自己有关的内容；没写清的地方，留下来再去问物业。
intro.connection: OpenAI（发布这篇说明的公司）讲过一件事：有人问 AI 一位做研究的人写的文章叫什么，AI 连着给了几个听着很肯定、却各不相同的回答。今天你也把通知交给 AI，再回到通知检查它说的每句话。

reference.label: OpenAI：AI 为什么会说没根据的话

sources.note: 问同一个问题，AI 给了几个听着很肯定、却互不相同的答案，提醒我们要回原文核对。
sources.summary: 作者描述了向一款广泛使用的聊天机器人询问某位研究人员的博士论文题目，却得到了数个语气笃定但各不相同的错误答案。作者区分了正确答案与毫无依据的猜测，并讨论了评估激励机制。
sources.limitation: 切勿虚构错误的论文题目，也不要在文中未指名的情况下指认具体的聊天机器人。该示例仅证实了所报告的那次失败案例，并不代表普遍的错误率。

reference.label: ChatGPT Search 发布介绍

sources.note: OpenAI 的历史产品公告。重点看：回答里的网页来源链接与可点开的来源列表。日期栏是公告发布日；所给来源记录的访问日是 2026 年 9 月 15 日。
sources.summary: OpenAI 在 2024 年 10 月 31 日介绍 ChatGPT Search：回答可以带网页来源链接，你能点开来源列表查看。
sources.limitation: 这是当年的发布介绍，不代表当前的功能或界面。有来源链接，不等于每条来源都支持回答里的每句话；你还是得打开对应内容核对。

reference.label: NASA：2022 年观月夜公告

sources.note: NASA 的历史公告。重点看：开头的活动日期与参与方式。日期栏是公告发表日；所给来源记录的访问日是 2026 年 9 月 15 日。
sources.summary: 公告发表于 2022 年 9 月 23 日，介绍的是 2022 年 10 月 1 日的观月夜。参与形式包括现场、线上，或者线上线下混合。
sources.limitation: 这是 2022 年的记录。不能把它的活动日期挪到 2023 年戈达德公告里，否则会拼出原公告里没有的活动通知。

reference.label: NASA：2023 年观月夜公告

sources.note: NASA 往期公告。重点看开头的邀请与参与信息。日期栏是发布日；来源记录的访问日是 2026 年 9 月 15 日。
sources.summary: 公告发布于 2023 年 10 月 16 日，邀请公众在 2023 年 10 月 21 日晚 6 点至 9 点（EDT，美国东部夏令时间），去马里兰州格林贝尔特的戈达德游客中心参加活动。活动风雨无阻，无需报名。
sources.limitation: 这是过去的活动安排，不是当下的邀请，也不能证明活动后来实际怎样举行。照着公告改写邀请只是教学练习，不代表 NASA 批准。未指定目标时区时，别直接换算 EDT 时间。

reference.label: 伦敦国家美术馆：计划参观

sources.note: 2026年9月18日查阅的官网资料。练习场景是假设，不是实时出行承诺。

materials.label: 物业发来的停车施工通知（练习）
materials.text: 【物业通知】各位业主：因 A 区地面车位重新划线及西侧道闸检修，9 月 27 日（周日）7:30—18:00，A 区地面车位暂停使用，A 区西门暂时关闭。A 区已停车辆请于 9 月 26 日（周六）22:00 前移至 B 区地下车库或小区外合法停车位。施工期间，B 区地下车库照常开放，请从东门进出。遇雨，划线工作顺延，具体时间将在业主群另行通知。为保证消防通道畅通，请勿占用消防通道。物业服务中心 9 月 24 日

materials.label: 你写给物业的情况说明（练习）
materials.text: 我家车停在 A 区地面，周日一早要送我妈去医院，平常从西门走。通知说下雨会顺延，那我周日还要不要先挪车？如果走东门，A 区的车能直接出去吗？

materials.label: 店铺售后说明（练习）
materials.text:
售后说明
1. 签收后 7 天内，商品完好、不影响二次销售的，可申请 7 天无理由退货；以物流签收时间为准。
2. 申请前请保留商品、配件、赠品和包装。已使用、通电、留下明显污渍或影响再次销售的，可能无法按无理由退货处理。
3. 食品、贴身用品、定制商品等，除质量问题外，不支持 7 天无理由退货。具体以商品详情页的特殊说明为准。
4. 商品有质量问题，请先上传照片或视频，客服会进一步处理。
客服服务时间：每天 9:00—22:00。

materials.label: 订单信息（练习）
materials.text:
商品：便携榨汁杯
签收：9 月 14 日
今天：9 月 19 日
情况：只打开外包装看过，未通电；杯体、充电线和说明书都在；外包装盒有一处折痕；商品详情页没有看到“不支持 7 天无理由”的特别说明。
你想申请退货，但不确定“打开过包装”和“盒子有折痕”会不会影响。

starter.prompt: 请根据这两段内容，帮我看看周日早上开车出门要注意什么。

predict.question: 看完两段材料，你猜 AI 会怎么处理通知没直接回答的地方？

options.label: 把通知写清的安排列出来，把剩下的问题留着。
根据 B 区地下车库能走东门，推断 A 区的车也一定能从东门出去。
只照着说施工日期，不管车停在哪、什么时候出门。

run.title: 先让 AI 读一遍通知
run.note: 刚才你猜了 AI 会不会补上没写的事。现在看回答：留意雨天和东门两处，看它有没有把原文说过头。
run.debrief: 你刚才猜了 AI 可能有三种做法。现在把你选的想法跟回答对照一下。拿到回答，先看它有没有把你的车和周日出门对上。再查两处：雨天，通知只说划线顺延、时间另行通知；东门，通知写的是 B 区地下车库走东门，可没写 A 区车能不能从东门出去。要是 AI 把没写的事说成定好的安排，就把那句话记成要问物业的问题。通知里找得到的，才可以照着办；找不到的，先问物业。要是这次没回答，先重新发一次；没有回答不能当成答案。

investigate.title: 哪些话能按通知照做？
investigate.brief: 刚才你要查的是雨天和东门两处。现在对着通知一句句核对，把下面的话分成“通知直接写了”和“通知没有这样说”。
investigate.explanation: 你刚才把原文和推测分开了。通知写了 A 区西门暂时关闭，就不能说成能正常出车；它只写 B 区地下车库走东门，没说 A 区的车能不能走东门。下雨是会顺延，但新时间得等物业通知。

more.question: 下雨后，什么时候能施工？
more.answer: 通知没给新时间。先看业主群的后续通知，或直接问物业。AI 能帮你写问题，但不能替物业定时间。

more.question: AI把两条原文拼成一句，怎么办？
more.answer: 把话拆开，一条条回通知里查。只要有一部分找不到原文，就先去问物业。

cards.text: 9 月 27 日（周日）7:30—18:00，A 区地面车位暂停使用。
cards.why: 通知原话写清了日期、时间和区域。

cards.text: 9 月 27 日早上，A 区车辆可以从西门正常开出。
cards.why: 通知说 A 区西门暂时关闭，从原文得不出这句话。

cards.text: A 区已停车辆要在 9 月 26 日（周六）22:00 前移走。
cards.why: 通知清楚写了车辆、日期和截止时间。

cards.text: 遇雨时，划线工作顺延，具体时间在业主群另行通知。
cards.why: 这是通知直接写清的雨天安排。

cards.text: B 区地下车库照常开放，进出从东门走。
cards.why: 通知把 B 区地下车库走东门的安排写在一起了。

cards.text: A 区的车可以直接从东门出去。
cards.why: 通知没说 A 区车辆怎么到东门，也没说能不能从东门出去。

modify.title: 让 AI 把没写的地方留下来
modify.brief: 刚才你把原文和推测分开了。现在只改原先的提问。留言里已经有了车位和出门时间，不用再写一遍。加上“写出原句”和“留下没写清的事”，让 AI 再答一次。
modify.goal: 请把我的出门安排和通知里的条件对上。通知里能找到的安排，写出原句；没说明的事，列成要问物业的问题。
modify.debrief: 你加的是核对办法，不是把留言重说一遍。拿到回答看两点：它有没有把你的情况和通知条件对上？有没有把找不到原文的地方列出来？要是这次没回答，先重新发，没有回答不能当成答案。如果它还把 A 区车能不能走东门说成确定事实，先把这话标出来。问题是回答越过了通知边界，不是你少写了一句话。

workbench.instruction: 只挑你觉得有用的短句放进去。留言里已经写了车位和时间。这些短句可以改、删，也能换顺序。

pieces.label: 分开写
pieces.text: 把通知写清的安排，和还要确认的事分开写。

pieces.label: 写出原句
pieces.text: 每条重要说法后，写出照着通知哪一句。

pieces.label: 留下问题
pieces.text: 通知没说清的事，列成要问物业的问题，别替我猜。

make.title: 换成退货，自己问客服
make.scenario: 现在换成网购退货。你收到一只便携榨汁杯。店铺规则和订单情况分在两段材料里。你想先弄明白能不能申请退货，再写一条发给客服的消息。
make.goal: 自己写提问，让 AI 对照两段材料。先分清已经知道的事实和还要问客服的地方，再写成一条退货咨询消息。
make.promptPlaceholder: 你想让客服确认什么？先说清商品、日期和使用情况。
checklist: 提问换成了榨汁杯订单和售后说明这件新事情。
成品留好了签收日期、通没通电、配件和包装等关键事实。
把规则说清的部分，和还要问客服的部分分开。
没有把材料没写的情况加进去。
make.artifactLabel: 发给商家的退货咨询消息

finish.title: 遇到长通知，先对条件
finish.note: 下次碰上长通知，先说清自己的时间和情况。再让 AI 把每句话对回原文。原文没写的，就去问负责的人。

lessons.title: 交给别人之前，这段请求还缺什么？
lessons.content:
# 交给别人之前，这段请求还缺什么？

## 给没到现场的朋友做一份回看说明

[美国国会图书馆的2024年国家图书节记录](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival)记载了当时公布的安排：活动定于2024年8月24日举行，部分节目将直播，全部节目的录像会后提供。你的朋友没能到现场，希望知道怎样了解这些节目。

你先写了一句请求：“请介绍这个图书节，写得自然，不要太长。”现在准备把它连同原页面交给助手。

## 先猜一下

与朋友真正要做的事情相比，这句请求还缺哪一项关键信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

它没有说明要给没到现场的人做回看导览。先把读者、成品和需要检查的范围说清楚，才知道哪种介绍真的有用。

## 自己写出一份可以照着做的请求

用三句话就可以开始：材料是哪一页；给谁做什么；成品必须保留哪些条件。你来写第一版，不必照抄一个万能格式。

写好后，对照原页面检查：“部分节目将直播”和“全部录像会后提供”有没有被混成一件事？历史年份有没有被改成现在？

:::detail[把这些要求都写进去，会不会变得太复杂？]
你不需要同时规定字号、语气、段落长度和几十条规则。先保留最影响这份成品的几项：朋友没到现场，目的是了解节目，材料是2024年的记录。然后把两种观看方式分开，免得一句话把“部分直播”改成“全部直播”。这几项都有用，因为它们决定朋友看完说明后会怎么理解。其他表达可以留给助手选择。你写完后也能直接检查，不必只说喜欢或不喜欢。[明确目标与相关背景的指导](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10032626-prompt-engineering-best-practices-for-chatgpt)可以支持这种写法，但这段请求和最终编辑稿都是我们自己的工作，不是图书馆的原文。
:::

把这份请求里的各部分放到正确的位置。它们分别告诉助手使用什么、交出什么、以及怎样算完成。

::play{#first-request-checkpoint-sort}

### 改一处，再保住已经对的部分

若第一版太长，就只要求缩短文字，并明确保留年份与观看范围。修改以后，用同一页面重新核对那两项。最后留下一份请求和一段你自己检查过的短说明。

:::detail[还没有实际运行助手，我现在能完成哪一部分？]
先写好请求与检查条件，再自己做一份简短编辑稿，也能发现要求是不是清楚。比如你写“介绍图书节”，却发现无论怎么缩短都不知道该删什么，往往是读者用途还没定；你写明给不能到场的人看，就知道优先说明回看方式。之后使用可用的助手时，再把真实结果放到同一条件下检查。没有运行工具的编辑稿，不叫模型实测；已经运行的结果，也不能因为读起来漂亮就跳过核对。你要带走的是一套可以由你判断对错的工作方式，而不是一次无法解释的好运气。
:::

:::detail[完成说明以后，应该把什么一起留下？]
保留你使用的原页面入口和最后一次检查的要点。这样，朋友追问哪句话从哪里来时，你能找到对应信息；你以后把说明改给另一种读者时，也知道哪些历史事实不能随手替换。无需保存所有试过的措辞，也不用把每次犹豫写成长报告。留下能帮助下一次继续工作的东西：成品、来源、仍需确认的事项。
:::

## 自检

现在把这份短说明改给只想挑选一个节目观看的人。请重新写一条请求，保留原材料，修改读者用途，并写出一个需要重新检查的条件。

## 一句话

**把材料、成品和检查条件连起来，你就能从“请帮我写”走到“我知道它是否写对”。**

en.title: Before Handing It to Someone Else, What Is This Request Still Missing?
en.content:
# Before Handing It to Someone Else, What Is This Request Still Missing?

## Write a Catch-Up Guide for a Friend Who Couldn't Attend

[The Library of Congress record of the 2024 National Book Festival](https://www.loc.gov/events/2024-national-book-festival) notes that the event was scheduled for August 24, 2024, that some sessions would be livestreamed, and that recordings of all sessions would be available after the event. Your friend was unable to attend in person and wants to know how to follow these programs.

You first write a request: “Please introduce this book festival. Write naturally and keep it fairly short.” Now you are ready to hand it over to the assistant along with the original page.

## Predict first
Compared to what your friend actually needs to do, which key piece of information is this request still missing?

Write down your judgment first before reading on to the answer.

## Answer
It doesn't explain that you are making a catch-up guide for someone who couldn't attend in person. Only by first clarifying the reader, the deliverable, and the scope to check can you know what kind of introduction is genuinely useful.

## Write an Actionable Request Yourself

You can start with just three sentences: which page the source material comes from; who you are making what for; and what conditions the deliverable must preserve. Write the first draft yourself—there's no need to copy a one-size-fits-all format.

Once written, check it against the original page: Were “some sessions would be livestreamed” and “all recordings would be available after the event” conflated into a single thing? Was the historical year changed to the present?

:::detail[Will including all these requirements make it too complicated?]
You don't need to specify font size, tone, paragraph length, and dozens of rules all at once. First, keep the few items that most affect this deliverable: your friend couldn't attend in person, the goal is to learn about the programs, and the source material is the 2024 record. Then separate the two viewing options so a single sentence doesn't turn “some livestreamed” into “all livestreamed.” These items are useful because they determine how your friend will understand the explanation after reading it. Other phrasing choices can be left to the assistant. Once you finish writing, you can also verify it directly, rather than just saying whether you like or dislike it. [Guidance on clarifying goals and relevant context](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10032626-prompt-engineering-best-practices-for-chatgpt) supports this approach, but this prompt and the final edited draft are our own work, not the library's original text.
:::

Put each part of this request into its correct position. They tell the assistant what to use, what to deliver, and what counts as finished.

::play{#first-request-checkpoint-sort}

### Change One Thing, Then Protect What Is Already Right

If the first draft is too long, simply ask to shorten the text while explicitly preserving the year and viewing scope. After making revisions, check those two items against the same source page again. Finally, keep one request and one short guide that you have verified yourself.

:::detail[Without actually running the assistant yet, which part can I complete right now?]
Drafting the request and check criteria first, and then creating a brief edited draft yourself, will also reveal whether your requirements are clear. For example, if you write “introduce the book festival” and find that no matter how you try to shorten it, you don't know what to cut, it's often because the reader's purpose hasn't been defined yet; when you clearly state that it is for someone who cannot attend, you know to prioritize explaining how to watch the recordings. Later, when you use an available assistant, you can check the real output under those same conditions. An edited draft created without running the tool does not count as an actual model test; nor should an output from an actual run skip verification just because it reads nicely. What you want to take away is a workflow where you can judge right from wrong yourself, rather than an unexplainable stroke of good luck.
:::

:::detail[After completing the guide, what should be kept alongside it?]
Keep the link to the original page you used and the key checkpoints from your final review. That way, if your friend asks where a certain statement came from, you can locate the corresponding information; when you adapt the guide for a different reader later on, you'll also know which historical facts cannot be casually swapped out. There is no need to save every phrasing you tried, nor to turn every hesitation into a lengthy report. Keep what helps you continue the work next time: the deliverable, the source, and any items that still need confirmation.
:::

## Check yourself
Now adapt this short guide for someone who only wants to pick a single program to watch. Rewrite the request: keep the original source material, change the reader's purpose, and write down one condition that needs to be rechecked.

## In one sentence
**Connect the source material, deliverable, and check criteria, and you can move from “please write this for me” to “I know whether it was written correctly.”**

lessons.title: 三个回答都很肯定，你该相信哪一个？
lessons.content:
# 三个回答都很肯定，你该相信哪一个？

## 同一个问题，出现了不同答案

[OpenAI 的一篇研究介绍](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/)记录过这样的情况：询问同一位研究者的博士论文题名，聊天工具给出了不同的肯定答案，而这些题名都不对。我们不需要再编三个假题名；真正的问题已经出现了——同一个事实被说成了几种不同版本。

## 先猜一下

如果你也遇到这种冲突，再让助手把答案说得更肯定，能补上哪一种缺少的信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

更肯定的语气不能补上论文的真实记录。你需要的是能够核对题名的材料，而不是另一种自信说法。

## 把“说得出来”与“查得到”分开

这类听起来像事实、实际没有对上事实的回答，常被叫作 AI 的“幻觉”。名字容易让人误会；你可以先把它理解成：它给出了具体说法，但没有相应依据支持。

先划出有冲突的那一项，再找能确认它的记录。暂时找不到，就把题名留作待核对，而不挑文风最好的一个。

:::detail[它说错了，是不是代表整份回答都不能用了？]
不一定。先把回答拆成你真正需要的几项，而不是一口气全信或全丢。论文题名不对，就不能把那个题名放进成品；文章的写作结构是否清楚，则可以另行判断。你也可以让助手把缺少依据的地方标出来，再围绕已核实的材料继续工作。这样，你没有因为一处错误而放弃所有帮助，也没有让一处写得顺的段落掩盖一个具体错误。关键是把错误定位到能检查的那一项。你现在知道它说出了多个版本，还不知道哪个事实成立，这正是应该补材料的位置，而不是要求它继续猜得更像真的。
:::

:::detail[为什么不能把几个答案投票，选最多的那个？]
重复出现的说法不一定来自新的证据。你连续问同一个工具，它可能仍然依靠同样的信息；即使换一种提问方式，也没有因此取得论文记录。投票能告诉你哪种说法出现得多，却不能替那种说法提供出处。你可以把不同答案当成提醒：这里值得查。但下一步应改变信息来源，比如找研究者本人或学校保存的论文资料，而不是只增加回答次数。这个方法也能用在其他任务上：同一张照片的日期出现冲突，就去看照片记录；同一场活动的时间不同，就去看对应活动的公告。所需的检查材料，取决于你正在判断的事实。
:::

把这些下一步动作分开：它们是在补充可核对材料，还是只改变回答的外观？

::play{#fluent-is-not-true-sort}

### 先处理那个没有依据的位置

你可以请求：“请指出题名来自哪份记录；若无法核对，就保留未知，不要补写。”这并不保证助手照做，但让你知道下一份结果要检查什么。

## 自检

同一张照片，两次回答给了不同的拍摄日期。你会寻找哪种材料，而不是再让它选一个日期？

## 一句话

**发生事实冲突时，补一份能核对的材料，比补一句更肯定的话更有用。**

en.title: Three Answers Are All Confident: Which One Should You Believe?
en.content:
# Three Answers Are All Confident: Which One Should You Believe?

## Different Answers to the Same Question

[An OpenAI research introduction](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/) recorded such a situation: when asked for the title of the same researcher's doctoral dissertation, a chat tool gave different, confident answers—and none of these titles were correct. We do not need to invent three more fake titles; the real problem has already emerged—the same fact was stated in several different versions.

## Predict first
If you also run into this kind of conflict, what missing information could be filled in by asking the assistant to sound even more confident?

Write down your judgment first before reading on to the answer.

## Answer
A more confident tone cannot supply the dissertation's actual record. What you need is material that allows you to verify the title, not another confident statement.

## Separate What Can Be Said from What Can Be Verified

Responses like these that sound like facts but do not actually match the facts are often called AI "hallucinations." The name can easily be misleading; for now, you can understand it as: it provides a specific claim, but without corresponding evidence to support it.

First mark the item where the conflict lies, then look for records that can confirm it. If you cannot find them for now, leave the title as pending verification rather than picking the one with the best writing style.

:::detail[If it got something wrong, does that mean the entire answer cannot be used?]
Not necessarily. First break down the response into the specific items you actually need, rather than trusting or discarding everything all at once. If the dissertation title is wrong, you cannot put that title into your final work; whether the writing structure of the article is clear can be evaluated separately. You can also ask the assistant to mark where evidence is lacking, and then continue working around the materials you have verified. This way, you don't abandon all help because of a single mistake, nor do you let a smoothly written passage cover up a specific error. The key is to isolate the error to the item that can be checked. You now know it has stated multiple versions and you do not yet know which fact holds true; this is precisely where you should add material, rather than asking it to keep guessing in a way that seems more real.
:::

:::detail[Why can't we vote on the answers and pick the most common one?]
A recurring claim does not necessarily come from new evidence. If you ask the same tool repeatedly, it may still rely on the same information; even if you rephrase your question, it still hasn't acquired dissertation records. Voting can tell you which claim appears more frequently, but it cannot provide a source for that claim. You can treat different answers as a reminder: this is worth checking. But the next step should be changing the information source—such as looking for dissertation materials kept by the researcher or the university—rather than simply increasing the number of responses. This method can also be used in other tasks: when dates for the same photograph conflict, look at the photo records; when times for the same event differ, look at the announcement for that event. The verification material required depends on the fact you are judging.
:::

Separate these next steps: are they adding verifiable material, or merely changing the appearance of the response?

::play{#fluent-is-not-true-sort}

### Address the Unsupported Point First

You can ask: "Please point out which record this title comes from; if it cannot be verified, leave it as unknown and do not make anything up." This does not guarantee the assistant will comply, but it lets you know what to check in the next result.

## Check yourself
Two answers give different capture dates for the same photograph. What kind of material would you look for, rather than having it pick a date again?

## In one sentence
**When factual conflicts arise, adding verifiable material is more useful than adding a more confident statement.**

lessons.title: AI 说你做得好，它检查过哪一项？
lessons.content:
# AI 说你做得好，它检查过哪一项？

## 一句夸奖，和一次逐项检查

[OpenAI 曾公开回滚一个过于迎合用户的更新](https://openai.com/index/sycophancy-in-gpt-4o/)。这个实际事件提醒我们注意一种区别。

你正在改写 [NASA 的历史观月公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)。下面两种评语是我们的编辑对照，不是那次事件中的模型原话：“写得非常好！”以及“日期还在，地点也在，但开始时间被删掉了。”

## 先猜一下

要判断这份改写是否保留了参加信息，你能从哪一种评语继续做出具体修改，为什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

第二种评语指出了检查过的项目和缺少的位置。第一种表达了赞同，却没有说明参加信息是否完整。

## 把喜欢与符合要求分开

你可以喜欢一段文字的语气，但它仍可能遗漏必要信息。先写下检查项，再要求助手逐项指出成品中的对应位置；缺了哪项，就写明缺了。

:::detail[是不是以后都不应该听AI的鼓励？]
鼓励可以帮助你继续写，问题在于不能把它当作另一种东西。你想知道这段话是否热情，语气评价有帮助；你想知道时间和地点是否保留，就要做内容核对。把两种需要分开，你不必拒绝所有赞美，也不会在被夸奖之后漏掉修改机会。比如一份通知读起来很自然，却少了时间，正确做法是保留已经写好的表达，再把必要信息补回去。如果每次听到“很好”就结束检查，错过的不是一个更严厉的老师，而是那一项实际没有被看过的条件。
:::

看两份编辑记录：一种只检查读起来是否自然，另一种检查参加信息。它们什么时候会作出相同判断？

::play{#agreement-is-not-a-check-contrast}

## 按你要的结果来提问

试写：“请按日期、地点、开始时间三项核对，把对应文字指出来；缺的项目直接写缺失。”检查结果出来后，你仍能自己对照原公告，而不只依赖它的评价。

:::detail[它逐项打了勾，就真的检查过了吗？]
打勾也可能只是另一种说法，所以最好同时要求给出对应位置。它说日期存在，你就在成品中找到日期；它说与原公告一致，你再对照原公告。这里的好处是检查变小了：你不再面对一句“整篇没问题”，而是面对三个能够分别确认的项目。若某项没有找到，就停在那一项修，而不是让它重新把整篇写得更漂亮。官方回滚事件只说明那次更新有迎合问题，不说明每个工具、每次鼓励都出错。你学到的检查方法，不靠猜助手是不是有意讨好你，而看它是否给出了可以继续核对的内容。

你还可以把检查写成一张小表：要求是什么，成品里哪句话满足它，原材料哪一处支持它。三列各做一件事；缺少对应位置就先留空，不把一个勾当成已经找到了文字。
:::

## 自检

你增加了“必须保留时区”这一项要求。昨天按日期、地点、时间完成的检查，还需要补哪一步？

## 一句话

**赞同说明它怎样评价你，逐项核对才说明成品是否符合要求。**

en.title: When the AI Says You Did Well, Which Item Did It Check?
en.content:
# When the AI Says You Did Well, Which Item Did It Check?

## A Compliment and an Item-by-Item Check

[OpenAI once publicly rolled back an update that was overly flattering to users](https://openai.com/index/sycophancy-in-gpt-4o/). This real-world incident reminds us to pay attention to a distinction.

You are rewriting [NASA's historical Moon observation announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/). The following two comments are our editorial comparisons, not the model's actual words from that incident: "Exceptionally well written!" and "The date is still here, and so is the location, but the start time was removed."

## Predict first
To judge whether this rewrite preserved the attendance information, which comment allows you to proceed with concrete revisions, and why?

Write down your judgment first before reading on for the answer.

## Answer
The second comment pointed out which items were checked and what was missing where. The first expressed approval, but did not indicate whether the attendance information was complete.

## Separating Liking from Meeting Requirements

You can like the tone of a passage, yet it may still omit essential information. First write down your checklist items, then ask the assistant to point out the corresponding locations in the final draft item by item; if an item is missing, state clearly that it is missing.

:::detail[Should you stop listening to AI encouragement altogether?]
Encouragement can help you keep writing; the problem is that you cannot mistake it for something else. If you want to know whether a passage sounds warm, an evaluation of tone is helpful; if you want to know whether the time and location were preserved, you must verify the content. By separating these two needs, you do not have to reject every compliment, nor will you miss an opportunity to revise after being praised. For example, if an announcement reads naturally but is missing the time, the right move is to keep the wording you have already written and add the necessary information back in. If you stop checking every time you hear "Looks great," what you miss out on is not a stricter teacher, but the specific requirement that was never actually reviewed.
:::

Look at two editorial logs: one checks only whether the text reads naturally, while the other checks the attendance information. When will they make the same judgment?

::play{#agreement-is-not-a-check-contrast}

## Ask for the Outcome You Want

Try writing: "Please check against the three items—date, location, and start time—and point out the corresponding text; for any missing item, state directly that it is missing." Once the check results come back, you can still cross-check against the original announcement yourself rather than relying solely on its evaluation.

:::detail[If it checked off every item, did it really inspect them?]
A checkmark can also just be another form of phrasing, so it is best to ask for the corresponding locations at the same time. If it says the date is present, locate the date in the final draft yourself; if it says it matches the original announcement, cross-reference the original announcement yourself. The advantage here is that the check becomes smaller: instead of facing a blanket statement like "the entire piece has no issues," you face three items that can each be verified independently. If an item cannot be found, stop and fix that specific item, rather than asking it to rewrite the entire piece to sound prettier. The official rollback incident shows only that that particular update had a sycophancy issue; it does not prove that every tool or every bit of encouragement is flawed. The checking method you learned does not rely on guessing whether the assistant is intentionally flattering you, but on whether it provides content that you can continue to verify.

You can also format the check into a small table: what the requirement is, which sentence in the draft satisfies it, and which part of the source material supports it. Each of the three columns serves one function; if a corresponding location is missing, leave it blank for now, rather than treating a checkmark as proof that the text was found.
:::

## Check yourself
You added a new requirement: "The time zone must be preserved." What additional step is needed for the check completed yesterday covering date, location, and time?

## In one sentence
**Approval shows how it evaluates you, while an item-by-item check shows whether the draft meets the requirements.**

lessons.title: 画得像历史照片，就真是历史吗？
lessons.content:
# 画得像历史照片，就真是历史吗？

## 一幅很像真的画，还缺什么

[Google 在 2024 年暂停了 Gemini 的人物图像生成](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/gemini-image-generation-issue/)，并公开说明某些结果存在历史不准确等问题。另一方面，[NASA 的《地出》页面](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/)把一张实际照片与摄影者、日期和任务记录放在一起。

你要给历史展板挑图，也要给一个虚构故事挑插画。两处都希望图片清楚、好看。

:::figure[《地出》：NASA / 阿波罗8号 / Bill Anders，1968年12月24日。官方图像，非AI生成。]{#earthrise}

:::

## 先猜一下

除了画得像不像，你会用哪一项不同要求来决定这两个位置分别适合什么图片？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

历史展板需要可核对的记录身份；虚构故事可以使用清楚标注的想象画。两者的差别不在于哪张更漂亮。

## 先决定图片在证明什么

如果图片要告诉读者“这件事真的这样发生过”，就要查来源、日期和图像身份。NASA 的照片记录能帮助你核对《地出》，不能顺带证明任何一幅风格相似的新画。

创作一幅想象场景则是另一种任务，关键是不要把它的身份藏起来。

:::detail[图像有机构名字，就可以不再检查了吗？]
还不能。你需要找到这张具体图像所在的记录，而不是只看到某个机构的名字。标题、图片与说明要对应，原图与改编图也要分开。比如你裁剪了《地出》的一部分，仍能说明它来自哪张原图；如果另画了原图里没有的物体，就不能再把整个新画面叫作那张原始照片。来源的作用是帮助你知道正在看什么，而不是替所有相似图像盖章。Google 的历史事件提供了一个真实提醒，但不证明今天所有生成图片都有同一问题；判断眼前这张图，仍然要检查眼前这张图的身份。
:::

给这两个用途选择合适的图像来源与标注方式。

::play{#a-picture-is-not-a-record-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

如果你的任务是为虚构故事表现一个想象中的世界，就没有必要把创意限制成一张历史照片。可以创作，但要让读者看得出这是插画或改编，而不是现场记录。

:::detail[真实照片也可能让人产生错误印象吗？]
可能。即使照片本身真实，把它放到错误的年份、地点或事件旁边，也会产生错误理解。你因此要同时检查图和图注，而不是只检查文件有没有被生成。比如《地出》拍摄于绕月任务，把图注写成月面着陆现场，就改变了这张照片的历史身份。相反，一幅明确写着想象插画的作品，不是在声称它记录了某次真实事件。你要分开的，是创作与记录两种用途，以及文字有没有让读者把它们混淆；这比简单地把图片分成“漂亮的可信，不漂亮的不可信”更能保护你的成品。

你给图片加标题时，可以先写它的身份，再写它想表达什么。原始照片、裁剪图、根据照片另画的插画，需要不同说明。不要因为它们都与同一主题有关，就在成品里只保留一个没有区分的来源标签。
:::

## 自检

你把一张真实照片改画成带有想象物体的画面。标题和图注需要怎样说明它的身份？

## 一句话

**图片可以帮助想象，也可以记录事实，但两种身份必须让读者分得开。**

en.title: If It Looks Like a Historical Photo, Is It Really History?
en.content:
# If It Looks Like a Historical Photo, Is It Really History?

## What Is Still Missing from an Image That Looks Real

[Google paused Gemini's image generation of people in 2024](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/gemini-image-generation-issue/), publicly explaining that some results had issues such as historical inaccuracies. On the other hand, [NASA's Earthrise page](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/) places an actual photograph alongside its photographer, date, and mission records.

You need to choose an image for a history display board, and you also need to select an illustration for a fictional story. In both cases, you want the pictures to be clear and appealing.

:::figure[Earthrise: NASA / Apollo 8 / Bill Anders, 24 December 1968. An official image, not AI-generated.]{#earthrise}

:::

## Predict first
Aside from how realistic it looks, what different requirement would you use to decide what kind of picture is suitable for each of these two placements?

Write down your judgment first before looking down at the answer.

## Answer
A history display board requires a verifiable record identity; a fictional story can use a clearly labeled imaginative drawing. The difference between the two is not about which one looks better.

## First Decide What the Image Is Proving

If an image is meant to tell readers that 'this really happened this way,' you must check its source, date, and image identity. NASA's photographic records help you verify Earthrise, but they cannot by extension prove any new picture in a similar style.

Creating an imagined scene is a different kind of task; the key is not to conceal its identity.

:::detail[If an image has an organization's name, can you stop checking?]
Not yet. You need to find the record containing this specific image, rather than merely seeing an organization's name. The title, image, and caption must correspond, and original images must be kept distinct from adapted ones. For example, if you crop a portion of Earthrise, you can still explain which original image it came from; if you draw objects not present in the original photo, you can no longer call the entire new image that original photograph. The purpose of a source is to help you know what you are looking at, not to rubber-stamp every similar image. The historical event with Google offers a real reminder, but it does not prove that all generated images today share the same issue; evaluating the picture in front of you still requires checking that specific picture's identity.
:::

Choose suitable image sources and labeling methods for these two uses.

::play{#a-picture-is-not-a-record-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

If your task is to depict an imagined world for a fictional story, there is no need to restrict your creativity to a historical photograph. You can create freely, but make sure readers can tell it is an illustration or an adaptation, rather than an on-the-scene record.

:::detail[Can an actual photo also create a false impression?]
It can. Even if the photograph itself is genuine, placing it next to the wrong year, location, or event will create a misunderstanding. You therefore need to inspect both the picture and the caption, rather than merely checking whether the file was generated. For example, Earthrise was taken during a lunar orbit mission; writing the caption as a lunar landing site changes the photograph's historical identity. Conversely, a work clearly labeled as an imaginative illustration is not claiming to record a real event. What you need to separate are the two purposes—creation and documentation—and whether the text leads readers to confuse them; this protects your finished work much better than simply dividing pictures into 'the attractive ones are credible, and the unattractive ones are not.'

When titling an image, you can state its identity first, and then describe what it aims to express. Original photographs, cropped images, and illustrations redrawn from photos require different explanations. Do not keep only a single, undifferentiated source tag in your final product just because they are all related to the same topic.
:::

## Check yourself
You redraw an actual photograph into a scene that includes imaginary objects. How should the title and caption explain its identity?

## In one sentence
**Images can support imagination and record facts, but readers must be able to tell the two identities apart.**

lessons.title: 同一个聊天框，为什么不总是在做同一件事？
lessons.content:
# 同一个聊天框，为什么不总是在做同一件事？

## 一个输入框，后面可能是不同动作

你在聊天框里提出请求，最后都看见一个回答。[搜索功能的介绍](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-search/)谈网页来源，[Whisper 的介绍](https://openai.com/index/whisper/)谈语音转写，而 [Google 的图像问题说明](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/gemini-image-generation-issue/)还特意区分了聊天应用、搜索与底层模型。

“聊天框”是你接触它们的地方，却不直接告诉你背后完成了哪种动作。

## 先猜一下

如果你要查一份新发布的公告，仅仅知道工具能写出一段流畅文字，还缺少哪一种能力信息？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

你还需要知道它能否找到或读取那份公告。会组织语言，不等于已经取得所需的新材料。

## 用动作理解工具能力

先不用背一串名称。找网页，是检索；把已有声音写下来，是转写；按要求形成新文字或图像，是生成。一个产品可能组合这些动作，但一次回答是否真的使用了某项能力，还要看实际过程和材料。

:::detail[为什么不把这些统称为AI就好了？]
日常交流时统称 AI 没问题，但你要判断任务能不能完成时，就需要更具体一点。你要寻找今天的新公告，关键是能否取得那份公告；你已经有一份录音，关键是能否处理声音；你想把公开资料改成一张简洁卡片，关键是能否按要求组织文字。它们最后都可能出现在聊天框里，检查方式却不同。把动作点名，你就能问到真正缺少的能力，而不必猜某个产品是不是“足够聪明”。你也不用了解它内部有多少程序；只需知道它拿了什么材料、做了什么变化、交回了什么成品。
:::

读每张任务卡，把它放到最直接完成这个动作的工具类别里。三个类别对应真实产品说明中的检索、转写与生成。

::play{#which-tool-did-it-use-sort}

## 它不是什么

工具名称不是这一次工作的证明。页面有搜索功能，不等于你正在读的每一句都已经搜索过；产品能处理音频，不等于任意回答都来自一段真实录音。

:::detail[我怎样看出这次到底做了什么？]
先找可以观察的线索。请求使用你上传的文件，就看看结果是否对应那份文件；要求找网页，就打开它给出的来源；要求转写，就用原录音核对相应位置。某些工具会显示使用过的动作，这可以帮助定位，但不能代替结果检查。若页面没有足够线索，就把范围问清楚，比如“这项日期是从我提供的公告提取的，还是你没拿到原文？”不要因为回答里出现“已经核实”几个字就停止。你要找的是任务与材料的对应关系，而不是一个听起来专业的标签。对于当前功能是否可用，也应查看当前说明，不把历史发布介绍当成永久保证。

你也可以先把任务拆成两句：先找到那份公告，再按公告写介绍。拆开以后，若第一步没有取得材料，第二步就不能偷偷把缺少的事实编进一段漂亮文字。
:::

## 自检

一个工具可以生成图片，但你现在需要当天发布的交通公告。你首先应确认哪一项与这次任务有关的能力？

## 一句话

**不要只问它是不是AI，要问它拿到什么材料、做了什么动作。**

en.title: Why Isn't the Same Chat Box Always Doing the Same Thing?
en.content:
# Why Isn't the Same Chat Box Always Doing the Same Thing?

## One Input Box May Involve Different Actions Behind It

You make a request in a chat box, and in the end, you always see an answer. [The introduction to search](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-search/) discusses web sources, [the introduction to Whisper](https://openai.com/index/whisper/) discusses speech transcription, and [Google's explanation of image generation issues](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/gemini-image-generation-issue/) even specifically distinguished chat apps, search, and the underlying model.

"The chat box" is where you interact with them, but it doesn't directly tell you which action was completed behind the scenes.

## Predict first
If you want to check a newly released announcement, and only know that a tool can write fluent text, what kind of capability information is still missing?

Write down your judgment first before reading the answer below.

## Answer
You also need to know whether it can find or read that announcement. Being able to organize language does not mean it has already retrieved the necessary new material.

## Understanding Tool Capabilities Through Actions

You don't need to memorize a long list of terms first. Finding web pages is retrieval; writing down existing audio is transcription; creating new text or images according to requirements is generation. A product may combine these actions, but whether an individual response actually used a given capability still depends on the actual process and materials.

:::detail[Why not just call all of this AI?]
Referring to it broadly as AI is fine in casual conversation, but when you need to judge whether a task can be completed, you need to be more specific. If you are looking for today's new announcement, the key is whether it can retrieve that announcement; if you already have an audio recording, the key is whether it can process audio; if you want to turn public material into a concise card, the key is whether it can organize text as requested. They may all end up appearing in a chat box, yet the ways to check them are different. By naming the action, you can ask about the capability that is truly missing, rather than having to guess whether a product is "smart enough." You also do not need to understand how many programs run inside it; you only need to know what materials it took in, what changes it made, and what finished product it returned.
:::

Read each task card and place it into the tool category that most directly performs this action. The three categories correspond to retrieval, transcription, and generation in real product descriptions.

::play{#which-tool-did-it-use-sort}

## What it is not

A tool's name is not proof of its work this time. Just because a page has a search feature does not mean every sentence you are reading was searched; just because a product can process audio does not mean an arbitrary answer comes from a real recording.

:::detail[How can I tell what was actually done this time?]
First, look for observable clues. If a request uses a file you uploaded, check whether the result corresponds to that file; if you asked it to find web pages, open the sources it provides; if you asked for transcription, check the corresponding locations against the original recording. Some tools display the actions that were used, which can help with locating them, but cannot replace verifying results. If the page does not have enough clues, clarify the scope, such as: "Was this date extracted from the announcement I provided, or did you not get the original text?" Do not stop just because the words "already verified" appear in the answer. What you are looking for is the correspondence between the task and the materials, not a professional-sounding label. As for whether a current feature is available, you should also check current documentation, rather than treating historical launch announcements as permanent guarantees.

You can also break the task into two sentences first: first find that announcement, then write an introduction based on the announcement. Once split, if the first step did not obtain the material, the second step cannot sneak the missing facts into beautifully written text.
:::

## Check yourself
A tool can generate images, but right now you need a traffic announcement released today. Which capability relevant to this task should you confirm first?

## In one sentence
**Do not just ask whether it is AI; ask what materials it received and what actions it took.**

# 表格排得整齐，合计就不会错吗？

## 几个大数字，数的却不是同一种东西

[史密森尼管理的开放数据集条目](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/)记录2020年开放发布超过280万件二维、三维图像，并在机构背景中另列210万册图书与15.6万立方英尺档案。

你想把它们整理成一个小表，有人却把这些行统一命名成“使用人数”。先不做计算，看看列名发生了什么变化。

## 先猜一下

这些数字都来自同一机构，为什么仍不能直接填进同一个“人数”列？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

因为它们数的是不同对象，单位也不同；没有一项是在记录独立的人。统一列名没有把图像、图书或档案体积变成人数。

## 先读列名，再看数字大小

给每行保留三个问题：数的是什么、单位是什么、对应哪个时点。发布图像有明确事件日，机构背景中的其他数没有逐项统计日期，不能顺手填成同一天。

[数据分析说明](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8437071)介绍了整理数据与检查分析的操作。表格整齐与数值含义正确，是两种不同检查。

:::detail[为什么数字抄对了，表格仍然可能错？]
你抄下210万，却把旁边的册改成人，这行字说的就是另一回事了。把15.6万立方英尺写成15.6万件也一样：体积与件数不是同一个计数单位。数字需要和对象、单位一起搬动，不能只复制中间的一串字符。这里不需要复杂数学就能检查：先用一句完整的话读出每一行，再问原文是否真的这么说。工具可以很快排表，但你仍要给表头一个与材料相符的含义。
:::

:::detail[图像与物品都可以叫“件”，为什么也不能直接合计？]
相同计量词并不证明两个集合互不重叠或一一对应。一件实物可以有不同角度的数字图像，数字资料也不一定等同于实物数量。当前条目没有给你完整对应表，就不要自行为它们创造一个合计对象。你仍能分别列出发布图像与馆藏背景，只是不能把看起来相似的单位当成合计依据。若真正需要回答数字化覆盖比例，应另查对象一致、范围明确的统计，而不是把手头两串数直接相除。
:::

:::detail[以后遇到浏览或下载次数，也要这样查吗？]
同样先看它数的是什么。一次浏览是动作记录，一个人可能产生多次动作；下载次数也不自动等于独立下载人数。这里不是在补报史密森尼的使用统计，而是把单位检查的方法带到另一类记录。你应先找有没有按人去重的定义，找不到就保留次数，不用猜成多少人。能指出缺少哪一项定义，就已经比把所有大数字排成一张“用户增长表”更接近真实问题。
:::

把真实条目直接支持的记录，与改换了对象或单位的说法分开。

::play{#numbers-need-a-check-sort}

## 自检

另一份记录只给浏览动作次数，没有说明如何去重。你还缺哪种信息，才能把它写成独立人数？

## 一句话

**数字先要回答数的是什么，再值得讨论算得对不对。**

en.title: If a table is neatly arranged, does that mean the total won't be wrong?
en.content:
# If a table is neatly arranged, does that mean the total won't be wrong?

## Several large numbers, but they do not count the same thing

An [open dataset entry managed by the Smithsonian](https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/) records the open release of more than 2.8 million 2D and 3D images in 2020, and separately lists 2.1 million books and 156,000 cubic feet of archives in the institutional background.

You want to organize them into a small table, but someone labels all these rows uniformly as "Number of Users." Without doing any calculations yet, look at what changed with the column names.

## Predict first
These numbers all come from the same institution, so why can they still not be entered directly into the same "Number of people" column?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
Because they count different objects and use different units; not a single one records individual people. Unifying the column name does not turn images, books, or archive volume into people.

## Read the column names first, then look at the numbers

Keep three questions for each row: what is being counted, what is the unit, and what point in time does it correspond to? The released images have a clear event date, but the other numbers in the institutional background do not have item-by-item statistical dates, so you cannot casually fill them in as the same day.

The [data analysis guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8437071) introduces steps for organizing data and checking analysis. A neat table and correct numerical meaning are two different checks.

:::detail[Why can a table still be wrong even if the numbers are copied correctly?]
If you copy down 2.1 million but change the "volumes" next to it to "people," that row says something completely different. Writing 156,000 cubic feet as 156,000 items is the same: volume and item count are not the same unit of measurement. Numbers must be moved together with their object and unit, rather than just copying the string of digits in the middle. You do not need complex math to check this: first read each row as a complete sentence, then ask whether the original text actually says that. Tools can format tables quickly, but you still need to give the header a meaning that matches the material.
:::

:::detail[Images and physical objects can both be called "items," so why can't they be totaled directly either?]
Using the same unit word does not prove that two sets do not overlap or correspond one-to-one. A single physical object can have digital images from different angles, and digital materials do not necessarily equal the number of physical items. Since the current entry does not give you a complete correspondence table, do not invent a combined total on your own. You can still list the released images and collection background separately; you just cannot treat seemingly similar units as a basis for totaling them. If you truly need to answer the digital coverage ratio, you should consult separate statistics with consistent objects and a clear scope, rather than simply dividing the two numbers at hand.
:::

:::detail[When encountering view or download counts in the future, should they be checked this way too?]
Similarly, look first at what is being counted. A view is an action record, and one person may generate multiple actions; download counts also do not automatically equal the number of unique downloaders. This is not about supplementing Smithsonian usage statistics, but about bringing the unit-checking method to another category of records. You should first look for a definition that deduplicates by person; if none is found, keep the action counts rather than guessing how many people they represent. Being able to point out which definition is missing already brings you closer to the real issue than arranging all large numbers into a "user growth table."
:::

Separate records directly supported by the original entry from claims that altered the object or unit.

::play{#numbers-need-a-check-sort}

## Check yourself
Another record gives only the number of view actions without explaining how they were deduplicated. What kind of information are you still missing before you can write it as a count of unique individuals?

## In one sentence
**A number must first answer what it is counting before it is worth discussing whether the calculation is correct.**

provenance.locator: 资料说明、管理者、许可与引用说明
provenance.supports: 由SI管理的数据集说明记录了2020年2月25日发布超过280万件CC0二维、三维图像及相关元数据和研究数据的事件。它在机构背景中另列1.55亿件物品、210万册图书和15.6万立方英尺档案，并标明管理者为SI。这些数量的对象与单位不同，不是独立使用人数。
provenance.limitations: 条目未给页面自身的发布日期。2020年日期属于发布事件；机构背景中的馆藏数没有逐项独立统计日期。不能把不同单位相加、推算数字化比例，或把这些数量写成下载量与人数。CC0说明针对所述数据集，不是网络上全部内容。

en.locator: Description, Managed By, License and How to Cite
en.supports: The SI-managed dataset description records the February 25, 2020 release of over 2.8 million CC0 2-D and 3-D images with related metadata and research data. It separately describes 155 million objects, 2.1 million library volumes and 156,000 cubic feet of archives in its institutional context. It names SI as manager. These are different kinds of quantities, not unique users.
en.limitations: The entry has no publication date for the page itself. The release date belongs to the release event; collection-context counts do not all have a separately stated census date. lessons.title: 试成功一次，下一次为什么还要检查？
lessons.content:
# 试成功一次，下一次为什么还要检查？

## 一个功能可以帮忙，也会遇到边界

[Be My Eyes 的照片助手介绍](https://www.bemyeyes.com/blog/introducing-be-my-ai/)说明了描述照片与继续追问的用法，并保留人工帮助。[关于错误回答的研究介绍](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/)则记录了具体事实回答失败的情况。

你已经用一份信息清楚的公开材料完成了图卡，现在换到一份关键日期看不清的扫描件。

:::figure[《地出》：NASA / 阿波罗8号 / Bill Anders，1968年12月24日。官方图像，非AI生成。]{#earthrise}

:::

## 先猜一下

前一份图卡做成了，为什么不能直接替这张新扫描件确认日期？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

因为新材料缺少你要检查的关键内容。前一次成功没有补上这一次看不清的日期。

## 保留方法，重新看条件

你可以继续使用“说明用途、提供材料、检查结果”这个方法，但要重新看材料是否足够。日期清楚时可以核对日期；日期缺失时，需要更清晰的原件或另一份记录。

:::detail[如果每次都要检查，学会方法还有什么用？]
方法让你知道应该检查哪里，而不是让你永远从头摸索。第一次你可能只会问“这是真的吗”，后来你能更快定位到“日期是否清楚”“来源是不是同一件事”“有没有把次数写成人数”。这些问题比重做所有工作小得多。前一次成功说明那一组材料与条件下，结果达到了要求；它也可以提供下一次的起点。但是换了材料后，原来足够的条件可能不再成立。你因此需要保留方法，而不是把某一次答案复制成永远适用的结论。这不等于每次都怀疑一切，而是把检查放在真正发生变化的地方。
:::

打开[NASA的《地出》照片记录](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/)。下面是对同一份材料的教学对照：一份保留日期，一份暂时遮住日期；不是另一次真实模型测试，也不是发现了另一份历史档案。先预测两种检查方法会不会给出相同结论。

::play{#one-good-example-contrast-brief-r2}

## 不够的信息，可以明确留空

若找不到清楚日期，就把那一项写成暂未核实，其他能够核对的内容仍可以继续整理。不要为了让图卡看起来完整，把一个猜测日期变成确定事实。

:::detail[怎样避免每次都把任务越做越大？]
先看那项未知是否影响当前成品。你在做只描述画面位置的卡片，拍摄日暂时未知，不一定挡住这句话；你在做按日期排序的历史档案，日期就是核心，不能略过。你可以把不同用途的完成条件写下来，需要时只补查影响当前用途的信息。这样，遇到未知不用做无休止的调查，也不会让你为了赶快结束而乱填。照片助手的发布说明与错误回答的研究，各自说明不同的真实情况；它们都不是对你手里这份新材料的验收。最后的检查仍要回到眼前的任务和输入。

先检查改变的部分，再决定是否需要扩大核对范围。
:::

:::detail[怎样保存一次有用的成功记录？]
记下当时有什么材料、要求交什么，以及你核对了哪几项。下一次任务变了，就能看见旧结果还能支持哪些判断。比如你记的是“有日期记录时，已核对图卡上的日期”，就不会把它误读成“没有日期时也可以猜出日期”。保存条件比只保存一个成功截图更容易帮助你重用方法。
:::

## 自检

同一份请求换成了更模糊的材料。你会保留哪一种使用方法，又重新检查哪一个条件？

## 一句话

**成功经验值得保留，但新材料的缺口仍要在这一次处理。**

en.title: If it worked once, why do you still need to check next time?
en.content:
# If it worked once, why do you still need to check next time?

## A feature can help, but it also encounters boundaries

[The introduction to the Be My Eyes photo assistant](https://www.bemyeyes.com/blog/introducing-be-my-ai/) explains how to describe photos and ask follow-up questions, while retaining human assistance. [The research introduction on incorrect answers](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/) documents cases where answers to specific facts failed.

You have already completed an image card using public material with clear information, and now you switch to a scan where the key date is illegible.

:::figure[Earthrise: NASA / Apollo 8 / Bill Anders, 24 December 1968. An official image, not AI-generated.]{#earthrise}

:::

## Predict first
If the previous image card was finished successfully, why can't you directly confirm the date for this new scan?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
Because the new material lacks the key content you need to check. The previous success did not make up for the date that is illegible this time.

## Keep the method, review the conditions

You can continue to use the method of "state the purpose, provide the materials, check the results," but you need to check again whether the materials are sufficient. When the date is clear, you can verify the date; when the date is missing, you need a clearer original or another record.

:::detail[If you have to check every time, what is the point of learning the method?]
The method tells you where to check, rather than leaving you to fumble from scratch forever. The first time, you might only ask, "Is this true?" Later, you can more quickly pinpoint questions like "Is the date clear?", "Are the sources referring to the same event?", and "Was a count of occurrences written as a headcount?" These questions are much smaller than redoing all the work from scratch. The previous success showed that under that specific set of materials and conditions, the result met the requirements; it can also provide a starting point for the next time. However, once the materials change, the conditions that were previously sufficient may no longer hold. Therefore, you need to keep the method rather than copy a one-time answer into a permanently valid conclusion. This does not mean doubting everything every time; it means focusing your checks on where things actually changed.
:::

Open [NASA's Earthrise photo record](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/). Below is a teaching comparison using the same material: one copy keeps the date, and one copy temporarily covers the date; this is not another real model test, nor is it the discovery of another historical archive. First predict whether the two checking methods will yield the same conclusion.

::play{#one-good-example-contrast-brief-r2}

## Insufficient information can be clearly left blank

If you cannot find a clear date, mark that item as not yet verified; you can still continue organizing the other content that can be verified. Do not turn a guessed date into a definite fact just to make the image card look complete.

:::detail[How do you avoid making the task bigger every time?]
First check whether that unknown affects the current finished product. If you are making a card that only describes positions in the picture, not knowing the shooting date for now does not necessarily block that statement; if you are making a historical archive sorted by date, the date is essential and cannot be skipped. You can write down completion criteria for different uses, and when needed, only look up additional information that affects the current use. That way, encountering an unknown will not require endless investigations, nor will it tempt you to fill in random guesses just to finish quickly. The release notes for the photo assistant and the research on incorrect answers each illustrate different real-world situations; neither is an acceptance check for the new material in your hands. The final check must still return to the task and input in front of you.

First check what changed, then decide whether you need to expand the scope of verification.
:::

:::detail[How do you keep a useful record of success?]
Note what materials were available at the time, what the deliverables required, and which items you verified. When the next task changes, you will be able to see which judgments the old result can still support. For example, if you noted "verified the date on the image card when a date record was available," you will not misread it as "dates can also be guessed when no date is available." Saving the conditions helps you reuse the method much more easily than saving only a screenshot of success.
:::

## Check yourself
The same request is now paired with blurrier material. Which method of use will you retain, and which condition will you re-check?

## In one sentence
**Successful experience is worth keeping, but gaps in new material still need to be handled this time.**

evidence.sourceTitle: Introducing: Be My AI

provenance.locator: 如何使用 Be My AI
provenance.supports: 2023年的公告描述了拍摄照片、获取描述并提出进一步问题的过程。当描述不够充分或需要核查时，仍有人类志愿者可供协助。
provenance.limitations: 这是一份面向盲人及低视力用户的历史厂商公告；它既非独立的准确性证据，也不构成对当前可用性的承诺。并未查验真实的用户记录。

en.locator: How to Use Be My AI
en.supports: The 2023 announcement describes taking a photo, receiving a description, and asking further questions. A human volunteer remains available when the description is insufficient or needs checking.
en.limitations: A historical vendor announcement for blind and low-vision users; not independent accuracy evidence or a promise of present-day availability. No actual user transcript was inspected.

evidence.sourceTitle: Why language models hallucinate

provenance.locator: 开篇示例与猜测动机解释
provenance.supports: 作者描述了向一款广泛使用的聊天机器人询问某位研究人员的博士论文题目，却得到了数个语气笃定但各不相同的错误答案。作者区分了正确答案与毫无依据的猜测，并讨论了评估激励机制。
provenance.limitations: 切勿虚构错误的论文题目，也不要在文中未指名的情况下指认具体的聊天机器人。该示例仅证实了所报告的那次失败案例，并不代表普遍的错误率。

en.locator: Opening example and explanation of guessing incentives
en.supports: The authors describe asking a widely used chatbot for a researcher's dissertation title and receiving different confident incorrect answers. They distinguish a correct answer from an unsupported guess and discuss evaluation incentives.
en.limitations: Do not invent the wrong titles or identify an unnamed chatbot. The example proves the reported failure, not a universal error rate.

lessons.title: 材料越多，回答就越贴近你吗？
lessons.content:
# 材料越多，回答就越贴近你吗？

## 两份都真实，哪份与问题有关

你手里有两份公开材料：[2023 年戈达德观月夜公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)，以及《地出》照片的记录。它们都与月球有关。你现在只想给一份历史活动介绍补上举办地点。

:::figure[《地出》：NASA / 阿波罗8号 / Bill Anders，1968年12月24日。官方图像，非AI生成。]{#earthrise}

:::

## 先猜一下

如果只先选一份材料，你会按什么理由决定，而不是把两份都塞进去？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

先选能回答当前问题的那一份。举办地点要回到活动公告，而不是因为照片也和月球有关就把它当作答案来源。

## 用问题挑材料，不用主题堆材料

先把问题缩成一句：“这场活动在哪里举行？”再检查每份材料是否真的提供这项信息。你不是在挑哪份资料更高级，而是在挑哪份与现在的任务对应。

:::detail[同一个主题的资料为什么也可能没用？]
因为主题比问题宽。活动公告与照片记录都可以被放进“月球”这个大主题，但它们分别记录不同的事情。你查的是活动地点，照片摄影者的信息再准确，也不能把这场活动安排到某个地址。[这份《地出》记录](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/)适合回答照片的拍摄身份，不适合回答戈达德某一场活动的举办信息。你可以先列一个问题，再在材料里找对应字段。找到的资料越具体，你之后需要检查的范围就越小。没有直接答案时，不要用同主题的段落凑出一个听起来相关的答复；把缺少的那一项找出来更有帮助。
:::

问题一变，选择也会变。为每个小任务选择最直接的那份材料。

::play{#choose-the-document-weigh}

## 什么时候该反过来

如果任务变成给照片写历史图注，就选照片记录。材料不需要永远分成好与坏；你换了问题，合适的材料也可以跟着换。

:::detail[什么时候确实应该同时用多份资料？]
当问题真的需要比较或连接它们时。例如你要做两张分别介绍照片与观月活动的卡片，两份材料各有位置；你要比较两年的活动日期，就需要两年的公告。多份资料有用的前提，是你知道每份在回答哪一个小问题。你可以把它们按问题分开放，而不是一次要求助手把所有内容揉成一段。[NotebookLM 最初的介绍](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/notebooklm-google-ai/)把用户选择的文档作为工作材料，这提供了一个清楚的使用思路：先选择材料，再围绕材料发问。但选择了材料并不保证回答没有错误，你仍然要检查回答是否真正来自选中的相应内容。
:::

## 自检

你的任务从介绍活动改成介绍照片摄影者。你会保留哪份材料，暂时移开哪份材料，为什么？

## 一句话

**选择材料的标准不是它也谈这个主题，而是它能回答眼前这个问题。**

en.title: Does More Material Make the Answer Closer to What You Need?
en.content:
# Does More Material Make the Answer Closer to What You Need?

## Both Are Authentic: Which One Is Relevant to the Question?

You have two public materials in hand: the [2023 Goddard Observe the Moon Night announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/), and the record of the "Earthrise" photograph. Both are related to the Moon. Right now, you only want to fill in the venue for an introduction to a historical event.

:::figure[Earthrise: NASA / Apollo 8 / Bill Anders, 24 December 1968. An official image, not AI-generated.]{#earthrise}

:::

## Predict first
If you could only pick one source first, on what grounds would you decide, rather than stuffing both in?

Write down your judgment first before scrolling down to see the answer.

## Answer
First choose the one that can answer the current question. For the event venue, go back to the event announcement, rather than treating the photo as a source of answers just because it is also related to the Moon.

## Pick materials by question, not by piling up a topic

First condense the question into one sentence: "Where is this event being held?" Then check whether each piece of material truly provides this information. You are not choosing which source is more advanced, but rather which one corresponds to the task at hand.

:::detail[Why might sources on the same topic still be unhelpful?]
Because a topic is broader than a question. Both the event announcement and the photo record can be placed under the broad topic of the "Moon," but they record different things. What you are looking up is the event location; no matter how accurate the photographer's information is, it cannot place this event at any address. [This "Earthrise" record](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/apollo-8-astronaut-bill-anders-captures-earthrise/) is suitable for answering the identity of who took the photo, but not for answering information about hosting a specific Goddard event. You can list a question first, then look for the corresponding field in the materials. The more specific the source you find, the smaller the scope you will need to check later. When there is no direct answer, do not piece together a plausible-sounding response from paragraphs on the same topic; identifying the missing item is far more helpful.
:::

When the question changes, the choice changes as well. Choose the most direct piece of material for each small task.

::play{#choose-the-document-weigh}

## When to choose the other way

If the task becomes writing a historical caption for the photo, choose the photo record. Materials do not need to be permanently categorized as good or bad; when you change the question, the appropriate material can change accordingly.

:::detail[When does it actually make sense to use multiple sources at once?]
When the question genuinely requires comparing or connecting them. For example, if you need to make two cards that separately introduce the photo and the Moon-observing event, each material has its place; if you want to compare event dates across two years, you need the announcements from both years. The prerequisite for multiple sources being useful is that you know which sub-question each one is answering. You can separate them by question rather than asking the assistant all at once to mash everything into a single paragraph. [The initial introduction of NotebookLM](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/notebooklm-google-ai/) uses documents selected by the user as source material, providing a clear way of thinking: choose the material first, then ask questions around it. But selecting the materials does not guarantee that the answers will be free of errors; you still need to verify whether the answers truly come from the corresponding selected content.
:::

## Check yourself
Your task changes from introducing the event to introducing the photographer of the photo. Which material would you keep, which would you temporarily set aside, and why?

## In one sentence
**The criterion for selecting material is not that it also discusses the topic, but that it can answer the question right in front of you.**

evidence.sourceTitle: Celebrate International Observe the Moon Night at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center

provenance.locator: 开篇邀请与参与信息
provenance.supports: 这份历史公告邀请公众于2023年10月21日美国东部夏令时间（EDT）晚6点至9点，前往马里兰州格林贝尔特的戈达德游客中心参加活动，风雨无阻，无需报名。活动内容包括日食艺术创作、太空岩石展示、用饼干演示月相以及月球着陆器设计活动。
provenance.limitations: 这是已经过去的过往活动，并非当前的活动邀请。本课程中重写的邀请函属于教学编辑练习，并非NASA官方批准的通知。在未指定目标时区的情况下，绝不可直接换算EDT时间。

en.locator: Opening invitation and participation information
en.supports: The historical announcement invited the public to Goddard's Visitor Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, on October 21, 2023, from 6 to 9 p.m. EDT, rain or shine. No registration was needed. Activities included eclipse art, space rocks, Moon phases using cookies, and a lunar-lander design activity.
en.limitations: Past event, not an invitation to attend now. A rewritten invitation in this course is an editorial exercise, not a NASA-approved notice. Never convert EDT without a specified destination zone.

lessons.title: 原文没有写的事，要让 AI 补上吗？
lessons.content:
# 原文没有写的事，要让 AI 补上吗？

## 公告说了无需报名，没有说完所有条件

[2023 年戈达德观月夜公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)给出了活动时间、地点，并写明无需报名。你想把这份历史材料整理成一张参加信息卡。手里这段材料没写每位访客的停车安排。

## 先猜一下

为了让卡片看起来完整，你能否把停车这一格直接写成“保证有位”，为什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

不能。没有找到这项安排，与确认保证有位是两回事；这一格应保留为未说明，或另找对应资料核对。

## 把空缺写清楚，比补得顺畅更有用

先分三种情况：原文明确写了，原文明确否定了，手里的材料没有说。这三个状态会让读者作出不同决定。

你可以请求：“只提取公告中已经写明的项目；没有写的标成未说明。”整理信息不是替原文增加承诺。

:::detail[未说明，和不提供服务有什么区别？]
未说明，是在描述你手里材料的范围；不提供，是在断言现实中的服务不存在。要作出后一种判断，需要相应记录支持。比如这段公告没有逐项介绍停车安排，你只能说这段材料没有交代，而不能据此断言现场一定没有停车，也不能反过来保证每个人都有位置。把这两种结论分开，你就不会因为一格空白而让整张卡失去可信度。你仍可以把时间和地点填好，只在停车这一项留下具体问题。读者因此知道哪些已经核对，哪些还需要另查，而不是面对一张看似完整、实际混进猜测的表。
:::

:::detail[怎样让助手别把空白补成听起来合理的话？]
把缺失时的处理方式写进请求，例如“没找到就写未说明，不使用一般经验补齐”。[文件任务的官方介绍](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8555545)区分了从资料提取内容与改写表达；你在做提取时，要保留原材料的边界。即便要求已经说清，也仍需抽查关键字段：那句保证来自原文哪一处？若它找不到位置，就不要把保证留在成品里。你也可以把待查项集中成一小段问题，之后向真正掌握安排的人询问。这里写的是历史资料卡，不能因为练习需要一个答案就替当年的主办方编出答复。
:::

根据这份公告已经给出的材料，把能填的项目与尚未给出的项目分开。

::play{#what-is-missing-sort}

## 自检

一份材料只写无需报名，你要整理费用栏。怎样写才能不把材料没说的费用都变成零？

## 一句话

**未说明是一种清楚的信息状态，不是让助手自由补写的空位。**

en.title: Should You Let AI Fill in What the Source Didn't Mention?
en.content:
# Should You Let AI Fill in What the Source Didn't Mention?

## The Announcement Said No Registration Was Required, but Did Not State All Conditions

The [2023 Goddard Observe the Moon Night announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/) gave the event's date, time, and location, and stated that no registration was required. You want to organize this historical material into an attendance information card. The material in hand does not mention parking arrangements for each visitor.

## Predict first
To make the card look complete, can you simply fill in the parking field as "Guaranteed space," and why?

Write down your judgment first before looking at the answer below.

## Answer
No. Not finding this arrangement is completely different from confirming a guaranteed space; this field should remain not specified, or you should find corresponding materials to verify it.

## Stating Gaps Clearly Is More Useful Than Filling Them Smoothly

First distinguish three situations: the original text explicitly states it, the original text explicitly denies it, or the material in hand does not say. These three states will lead readers to make different decisions.

You can request: "Extract only items already stated in the announcement; mark anything not written as not specified." Organizing information is not about adding commitments on behalf of the original text.

:::detail[What is the difference between "not specified" and "not providing the service"?]
"Not specified" describes the scope of the material in your hands; "not provided" asserts that the service does not exist in reality. Making the latter judgment requires supporting records. For example, because this announcement does not introduce parking arrangements item by item, you can only say that this material does not mention them; you cannot assert from this that there is definitely no parking on site, nor can you turn around and guarantee that everyone has a space. By separating these two conclusions, you avoid letting a single blank field undermine the credibility of the entire card. You can still fill in the time and location, leaving a specific question only for parking. Readers will therefore know what has been verified and what still needs to be checked separately, rather than facing a table that looks complete but actually smuggles in guesses.
:::

:::detail[How do you keep the assistant from filling in blanks with plausible-sounding statements?]
Include instructions for handling missing information in your prompt, such as "if not found, write not specified; do not use general experience to fill it in." The [official introduction to file tasks](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8555545) distinguishes extracting content from materials from rewriting expressions; when doing extraction, you must preserve the boundaries of the source material. Even if requirements have been clearly stated, you still need to spot-check key fields: where in the original text does that guarantee come from? If it cannot be located anywhere, do not keep that guarantee in the finished product. You can also gather items to be checked into a short list of questions to ask someone who actually knows the arrangements later. This is a historical information card; you cannot make up an answer on behalf of that year's organizers just because an exercise requires one.
:::

Based on the material already provided in this announcement, separate the items that can be filled in from those not yet given.

::play{#what-is-missing-sort}

## Check yourself
A document only states that no registration is required, and you need to organize the fee column. How can you write it so you don't turn fees not mentioned in the material into zero?

## In one sentence
**"Not specified" is a clear state of information, not a blank space for the assistant to fill in freely.**

lessons.title: 两份标题很像的公告，能直接拼在一起吗？
lessons.content:
# 两份标题很像的公告，能直接拼在一起吗？

## 两个日期，都在各自的原文里

[2022 年的公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-with-nasa/)指向 10 月 1 日的观月夜，[2023 年的公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)指向 10 月 21 日的活动。你想整理一个两年活动的小索引。两份材料都是真的，也都出现月亮和 NASA。

## 先猜一下

如果把较短的标题、较新的年份和较早的日期各取一个，拼成一行，会失去哪一项重要关系？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

会丢掉每个字段与原来那场活动的对应关系。拼出来的一行可能从未在任何一份公告里出现过。

## 让一行只指向同一件事

先给每行保留年份，再把该年的活动日期与来源放在同一行。2022 年的日期属于 2022 年记录，2023 年的日期属于 2023 年记录。

整理可以改变排列方式，但不能拆散事实属于谁。

:::detail[都是同名活动，为什么还要分两行？]
因为你要回答的不只是活动叫什么，还要回答哪一次、什么时候。一个活动名称可以多年重复出现，日期和安排却可能改变。两份资料的共同名称帮助你把它们放进同一个主题，但不能把所有字段混成同一个事件。你可以先为每行加一个读者能懂的身份，比如“2022 年观月夜”和“2023 年戈达德活动”，再填相应日期。读者之后想核对其中一项时，就知道该打开哪份原文。如果把来源只放在整张表的底部，却没告诉人每行对应哪条，表格看起来简洁，核对工作反而变难。
:::

在两个给定资料列表中，比较整行保留与随手拼字段的结果。

::play{#two-years-two-events-contrast}

## 合并介绍，不等于合并身份

你可以写一句“两年都举行了观月活动”，也可以并排介绍它们；但具体日期仍要各有归属。概括共同点时，不要顺手把差异抹掉。

:::detail[资料发生更新时，也照这个办法处理吗？]
先确认变化发生在同一事件的新版本，还是另一个事件。前者可能需要记录原安排和更新后的安排，后者则应保留两个不同对象。你不能只看到一个日期较新，就把旧资料里的所有字段都当成失效；也不能只因标题相同，就认定它们说的是同一次。可以让助手先列出对象、时间、来源三项，再说哪些地方一致、哪些不同。缺少能判断版本关系的说明时，就明确标出暂不能判断，而不是自动选择一个顺眼的组合。这个步骤把比较与拼接分开，让你有机会在混淆发生之前发现它。
:::

:::detail[两个年份都是真的，为什么不能选一个更熟悉的？]
因为真实并不等于适用。你正在回答某一年的活动问题，另一年的安排即使完全正确，也不能替它作答。先在草稿旁写出“我现在整理的是哪一年”，再核对日期、地点和参加方式是否出自同一条记录。如果要比较两个年份，就保留两行，并把每行的出处放在旁边。这样读者能看清两场活动各自的安排，不会把你的比较表误读成一张真实存在过的活动通知。
:::

## 自检

官网出现了新日期，旧邀请里仍是原日期。你需要先确认这是同一次活动的更新，还是两次活动的哪一种关系？

## 一句话

**整理可以改变文字的位置，但不能改变每项事实原本属于谁。**

en.title: Can Two Announcements with Similar Titles Be Directly Pieced Together?
en.content:
# Can Two Announcements with Similar Titles Be Directly Pieced Together?

## Two Dates, Each in Its Own Original Text

The [2022 announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-with-nasa/) points to the October 1 Moon Observation Night, and the [2023 announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/) points to an October 21 event. You want to compile a small index of events across the two years. Both materials are genuine, and both feature the Moon and NASA.

## Predict first
If you take one shorter title, one newer year, and one earlier date, and piece them into a single row, which important relationship is lost?

Write down your judgment first, then look below for the answer.

## Answer
You lose the correspondence between each field and the original event. The resulting spliced row may never have appeared in either announcement.

## Let Each Row Point to Only One Event

First retain the year for each row, then place that year's event date and source on the same row. The 2022 date belongs to the 2022 record, and the 2023 date belongs to the 2023 record.

Organizing can change the arrangement, but it cannot break apart who the facts belong to.

:::detail[Both events have the same name, so why split them into two rows?]
Because you need to answer not just what the event is called, but which occurrence and when. An event name can repeat across multiple years, but dates and arrangements may change. The shared name between the two sources helps you place them under the same topic, but it does not let you blend all fields into a single event. You can first give each row an identity that readers will understand, such as "2022 Moon Observation Night" and "2023 Goddard Event," and then fill in the corresponding dates. When readers want to verify one of the entries later, they will know which original text to open. If you place the sources only at the bottom of the entire table without telling people which row corresponds to which source, the table may look clean, but verification actually becomes harder.
:::

In the two given source lists, compare the results of keeping entire rows intact versus casually cobbling fields together.

::play{#two-years-two-events-contrast}

## Introducing Them Together Does Not Mean Merging Their Identities

You can write a sentence like "Moon observation events were held in both years," or introduce them side by side; but specific dates must still each belong to their own record. When summarizing common ground, do not casually erase differences.

:::detail[Do you handle it the same way when information is updated?]
First determine whether the change occurs in a new version of the same event or in a different event altogether. The former may require recording both the original arrangement and the updated arrangement, while the latter should preserve two distinct entities. You cannot simply see a newer date and treat all fields in the older material as invalid; nor can you assume they refer to the exact same occurrence just because the titles match. You can have an assistant first list three items—entity, time, and source—and then explain where they align and where they differ. When context for determining version relationships is missing, clearly label it as indeterminable for now, rather than automatically choosing a combination that looks pleasing. This step separates comparison from splicing, giving you a chance to spot confusion before it happens.
:::

:::detail[Both years are real, so why can't I just pick the more familiar one?]
Because being real does not mean being applicable. You are answering a question about an event from a particular year; another year's arrangements cannot answer for it, even if they are completely accurate. First write beside your draft "which year am I currently compiling," then verify whether the date, location, and participation details all come from the same record. If you need to compare two different years, keep two rows and place each row's source right beside it. That way, readers can clearly see the distinct arrangements for each of the two events and will not misread your comparison table as an event notice that actually existed.
:::

## Check yourself
A new date has appeared on the official website, while the original date is still shown in the old invitation. Do you first need to confirm whether this is an update to the same event, or which relationship applies between two separate events?

## In one sentence
**Organizing can change the position of words, but it cannot change who each fact originally belongs to.**

lessons.title: 资料里写着命令，助手就该照做吗？
lessons.content:
# 资料里写着命令，助手就该照做吗？

## 材料里也会出现“请你做这件事”

你让助手总结 [一则公开活动公告](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/)。公告邀请读者参加，还给出了相关入口。你自己的任务却只是整理历史信息。

[Agent 的官方介绍](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-agent/)也讨论了另一种风险：外部网页中的指令可能试图改变助手原来的任务。

## 先猜一下

公告里出现参加邀请，是否就表示你已经让助手替你参加或报名，为什么？

先写下你的判断，再往下看答案。

## 答案

没有。被阅读的材料与给助手的授权不同；总结一份邀请，不等于接受邀请并执行其中的动作。

## 先看这句话是谁对谁说的

你交代给助手的是任务。公告中的话是要被理解和总结的内容。两处都可以出现“请”，但它们在这次工作中扮演不同角色。

把外部材料里的话误当成新的任务要求，就可能让助手偏离你原本要做的事。

:::detail[材料中的邀请是不是都不该理会？]
不是。你需要读懂邀请，才能准确总结它；不需要因为看见邀请，就把它变成自己的行动。比如公告写欢迎参加，你可以在摘要里说明它面向公众，却不因此替自己建立报名记录。你要整理的是文字的意思，执行报名则是另一项任务。这个区别也适用于网页上的订阅提示、下载按钮和联系邀请：它们可能是有用信息，也可能只是页面的一部分。先问“我现在被要求分析它，还是已经被授权执行它”，就能分清角色。这里不需要把所有外部文字都当成恶意，只需要不让来源位置悄悄变成授权位置。
:::

把这次工作中的话分清楚：哪些是你的任务要求，哪些只是要分析的材料？

::play{#quote-or-instruction-sort}

## 它不是什么

“读懂资料”不是“服从资料”。你也不能只靠一句“忽略外部指令”就保证所有工具安全；涉及真实文件或对外动作时，还需要实际权限与确认机制。

:::detail[我想让助手真的照公告做事，应该怎样表达？]
另起一项明确任务，把动作、对象和范围说清楚。写草稿、查看信息、提交资料、发出消息，后果各不相同。你可以先允许它准备草稿，检查完了再决定是否发送；原公告中的“欢迎报名”并没有替你作这个决定。Agent 的介绍展示了确认、暂停和接管等控制思路，同时也承认外部指令带来的风险。你使用具体工具时，需要确认它实际提供哪些控制，而不是因为读过一段说明就认为任何自动动作都可放心交出去。判断权限时，始终回到你真正说过的任务，而不是它正在读取的网页里恰好出现了什么命令。
:::

:::detail[材料里真的有一条命令，也不能照做吗？]
先看你交代的任务。你要整理一份说明，就可以把其中的命令解释给读者；你没有因此授权工具去执行它。阅读一份要求删除文件的材料，与同意删除你的文件，属于两个不同的决定。需要执行时，也应由有权决定的人确认目标与范围，而不是把“材料写了什么”自动当作“现在可以做什么”。
:::

## 自检

你让助手整理一份活动说明，页面里有订阅通知。怎样判断这次任务有没有包含实际订阅？

## 一句话

**资料里的命令可以被理解，但只有你明确交代的任务才能成为这次工作的授权。**

# If Reference Material Contains a Command, Should the Assistant Follow It?

## "Please Do This" Can Also Appear in Reference Material

You ask an assistant to summarize [a public event announcement](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/celebrate-international-observe-the-moon-night-at-nasas-goddard-space-flight-center/). The announcement invites readers to attend and provides relevant links. Your own task, however, is merely to compile historical information.

[The official introduction to Agents](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-agent/) also discusses another risk: instructions on external web pages may attempt to alter the assistant's original task.

## Predict first
Does the appearance of an invitation to attend in the announcement mean you have already told the assistant to attend or register on your behalf, and why?

Write down your judgment first before reading the answer below.

## Answer
No. Material being read is different from authorization granted to the assistant; summarizing an invitation is not equivalent to accepting the invitation and carrying out its actions.

## First Look at Who Is Speaking to Whom

What you assign to the assistant is a task. The words in the announcement are content to be understood and summarized. The word "please" can appear in both places, but they play different roles in this workflow.

Mistaking statements in external materials for new task requirements can cause the assistant to stray from what you originally intended to do.

:::detail[Should invitations in materials be completely ignored?]
No. You need to understand the invitation to summarize it accurately; you do not need to turn it into your own action just because you saw it. For example, if an announcement says attendees are welcome, you can explain in the summary that it is open to the public without creating a registration record for yourself. What you are organizing is the meaning of the text; executing the registration is a separate task. This distinction also applies to subscription prompts, download buttons, and contact invitations on web pages: they may be useful information, or they may simply be part of the page. Asking first, "Am I currently asked to analyze this, or have I been authorized to execute it?" makes it possible to distinguish between roles. There is no need to treat all external text as malicious here; you simply must not let the location of a source quietly turn into a location of authorization.
:::

Distinguish the statements in this workflow: which are your task requirements, and which are merely materials to be analyzed?

::play{#quote-or-instruction-sort}

## What it is not

"Understanding reference material" is not "obeying reference material." Nor can you ensure the safety of all tools merely with a phrase like "ignore external instructions"; when real files or external actions are involved, actual permissions and confirmation mechanisms are also required.

:::detail[If I want the assistant to actually act on the announcement, how should I express that?]
Start a separate, explicit task that clearly states the action, target, and scope. Drafting, viewing information, submitting materials, and sending messages carry very different consequences. You can first allow it to prepare a draft, and then decide whether to send it after reviewing; the "welcome to register" in the original announcement did not make this decision for you. The Agent introduction illustrates control approaches such as confirmation, pausing, and takeovers, while also acknowledging the risks posed by external instructions. When using specific tools, you need to verify what controls they actually provide, rather than assuming any automated action can be safely handed over just because you read a description. When assessing authorization, always return to the task you actually stated, rather than whatever command happens to appear on the web page it is reading.
:::

:::detail[If there really is a command in the material, should it still not be followed?]
First look at the task you assigned. If you need to organize an explanation, you can explain the command within it to the reader; you have not thereby authorized the tool to execute it. Reading material that asks to delete files and agreeing to delete your files are two different decisions. When execution is required, someone with decision-making authority should confirm the target and scope, rather than automatically treating "what the material says" as "what may be done now."
:::

## Check yourself
You ask an assistant to compile an event guide, and the page contains a subscription notice. How do you determine whether this task includes an actual subscription?

## In one sentence
**Commands in reference material can be understood, but only tasks you explicitly assign serve as authorization for the work.**
